newsitem.title: UK: Cuban missile crisis highlights Cyprus troubles.
newsitem.headline: Cuban missile crisis highlights Cyprus troubles.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent

The latest flareup between Greece and Turkey shows how the threats to peace have changed since a similar crisis about an island and some missiles pushed the world to the brink of nuclear war more than 30 years ago.

The 1962 Cuban missile crisis, when the United States forced the Soviet Union to withdraw weapons it had deployed on the communist island state, was perhaps the most memorable and dangerous standoff of the Cold War era.
Now, halfway around the world, Turkey is warning that it may use force to stop the deployment of Russian anti-aircraft missiles purchased by the Greek Cypriot government.
The stakes are clearly not as high as with Cuba, not least because the missiles will not be delivered until mid-1998.

But the recent deterioration of relations between Greece and Turkey highlights how other dangers have replaced fears of global nuclear holocaust -- indeed, partly because the threat of complete annihilation is no longer with us.
Cyprus, divided since 1974 when Turkish forces invaded and occupied the northern third of the island, was little more than a sideshow during the years of East-West confrontation.
Both Greece and Turkey, as members of NATO, could not afford to let their rivalry spill over into open conflict in the face of the military threat from the Warsaw Pact.
"A war between two NATO allies would have been unthinkable in the face of the Soviet threat," said one European diplomat involved in trying to ease current Greek-Turkish tensions.
"We have become aware that it is now all too possible."

Since the collapse of the Berlin Wall in 1989, conflicts based on long-suppressed ethnic, religious and historical differences have burst into the open -- freed at last from the constraints of the Cold War.
From the collapse of Yugoslavia to the ethnic slaughter in Central Africa, strategic concerns have crumbled and messy wars have broken out within states, rather than between them.

The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) listed 30 major conflicts around the world in its 1996 report, all of them primarily internal and many in places that the major powers no longer considered important.
It was, SIPRI said, "a new post-Cold War reality in which governments have started to lose control of developments".
So far, Western powers have prevented such conflicts "spilling over", so that other countries are drawn into them.

During four years of war in former Yugoslavia, the United States and its allies put much effort into stopping the conflict spreading south to Greece, knowing that it could also draw in Turkey if that happened.
Cyprus reinforces that concern. It is the point at which two rival and inimical cultures meet across a thin line -- the Moslem Turks and the Orthodox Greeks.

A military conflict between Greece and Turkey would be serious enough, but there would also be political and diplomatic "spillover" into sensitive areas as plans to reshape European security forge ahead.

Greece could damage European Union business as the bloc finalises plans for a single currency and for new members to join, while either side could veto NATO projects, including enlargement into Eastern Europe.
Solving such problems in the late 1990s is infinitely more complicated and confused than it was during the Cuban missile crisis, an issue resolved solely by Moscow and Washington.

The United States is the only remaining superpower, but Russia is keen to make its voice heard and the European Union is struggling to build a place for itself on the world stage -- whether dealing with Cyprus, Yugoslavia or the Middle East.
As a result, each crisis brings various countries to jockey for position, often in competition even as they promise to cooperate in finding a solution.

Diplomats say this is also true of Cyprus, where European allies are worried that the United States may try a new initiative of its own, undermining a U.N.-backed plan to resolve the island's conflict by turning it into a federal state.
The picture is further complicated by the fact that Greece is a member of the 15-nation European Union while Turkey is not.

Ankara feels increasingly abandoned by Western partners who no longer assign it the same strategic value as they did during the Cold War, when it was one of only two NATO allies that shared a border with the Soviet Union.
